source: Majumder et al. (2024) DiscoveryBench: Towards data-driven discovery with LLMs
finding: Re-read the exact paragraph on domain knowledge. The sentence says performance jumps 'from 9.9% (w/ domain knowledge) to 17.5% (w/o)'. The verb 'jumps' and the stated purpose (check whether added domain knowledge helps) mean the labels are swapped: 9.9% is without hints and 17.5% is with hints. Gap 4 direction: hints help. Only v1 of the arXiv paper was served, so no later correction could confirm this.
numbers: DataVoyager (GPT-4p), archaeology tasks that needed domain knowledge: 9.9% to 17.5%, a gain of 7.6 points on a subset. Subset size is not stated in the passage. Best non-oracle agent overall 25%; biology 0%, engineering 7%, economics 25%, sociology 23%.
quote: performance jumps from 9.9% (w/ domain knowledge) to 17.5% (w/o domain knowledge)
limits: Direction is inferred from wording, not from a table. Subset N not given. One model, one task family. No error bars in the passage.
agent_relevance: Hints can lift a weak agent on knowledge-heavy tasks, but from a very low base. Treat as a modest, unverified gain.

source: Zheng et al. (2026, ICLR) NewtonBench: Benchmarking generalizable scientific law discovery in LLM agents
finding: 324 law-discovery tasks in 12 physics domains. Laws are counterfactually shifted so the model cannot recite them, and the agent must probe a simulated system by experiment. Eleven LLMs tested. Ability is clear but fragile: it falls with system complexity and with noise. Weak non-reasoning models stay under 10 percent overall.
numbers: Weak models (GPT-4.1-mini, GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3): overall symbolic accuracy below 10%, 20-40% on the simplest setting. Strong reasoning models 30-80% overall; GPT-5 75.9%, Gemini-2.5-pro 65.4%. Hardest setting: GPT-5 40.3%, Gemini-2.5-pro 16.7%, all other reasoning models under 6%. Domain range 18% (Bose-Einstein) to 54%. Symbolic accuracy is judged by an LLM with 98.3% agreement with human experts.
limits: Judge is an LLM. Benchmark is physics only. Counterfactual shifts change plausibility. No signal-to-operator table was tested; arms are vanilla vs code interpreter only.
agent_relevance: Fresh, memorisation-resistant, interactive law tasks exist now. This is the right testbed for gap 1 (a BACON-style table arm vs free reasoning). Gap 1 is still untested, but the harness is available.

source: Zheng et al. (2026) NewtonBench, noise, code-tool and PySR analyses
finding: Three side findings. (1) Noise: even 0.0001 Gaussian noise cut symbolic accuracy by 12-16% relative to noise-free; accuracy fell steadily to noise 0.1 while fit error (RMSLE) stayed flat. (2) A code interpreter helps weak models and slightly hurts strong ones, because the strong models stop exploring and settle early. (3) PySR, a classic search, matched or beat non-reasoning LLMs on symbolic accuracy but stayed well below reasoning models.
numbers: Noise test on GPT-5-mini at 0.0001, 0.001, 0.01, 0.1. Code effect flips at about 40% baseline symbolic accuracy. Going from 0 to 1 code call already degrades Gemini-2.5-flash and GPT-5-mini.
limits: Noise experiment is one model. The figure gives noise values, not a table, so exact numbers per level were not read. PySR was tested only on the vanilla equation setting.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a noisy checker lets numeric fit look fine while the exact form is lost. Score the form, not just the fit. A tool that makes checking easy can cut exploration; cap early exploitation.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Repeated sampling raises coverage (the share of problems with at least one correct sample) smoothly, but turning coverage into answers needs a verifier. With an automatic verifier (unit tests, proof checker) the gain is real. Without one, majority voting and reward models stop improving after about 100 samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite, DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample, 56% with 250 samples (single-sample SOTA 43%). MATH, Llama-3-8B-Instruct: coverage 82.9% at 100 samples to 98.44% at 10,000; majority vote or reward-model selection only 40.50% to 41.41% over the same range. Manual check of 105 GSM8K chains of thought: over 90% faithful, so signal exists for a better verifier.
quote: common approaches to verification plateau beyond approximately 100 samples
limits: Selection methods tested were majority vote and one 8B reward model (ArmoRM). Stronger verifiers might do better. On software tasks unit tests can pass wrong code (false positives).
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the LaSR / LLM-SR style gain depends on a strong checker. With a weak or absent one, more candidates mostly widen the gap between what the model can produce and what it can pick.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: With a learned process reward model (PRM) as the checker, more search helps on hard questions and hurts on easy ones, because stronger optimisation exploits errors in the checker. Beam search degrades as budget grows on easy MATH questions (levels 1-2) but beats best-of-N on levels 3-4. On level 5 nothing makes real progress.
numbers: Compute-optimal allocation by question difficulty matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute. FLOPs-matched: where a small model has non-trivial success, test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model. Easy questions do best with fully sequential revisions; hard ones need a balance of sequential and parallel.
quote: beam search, degrades performance as the generation budget increases, suggesting signs of exploitation of the PRM signal
limits: MATH only, PaLM 2 variants, PRM trained by the authors. The 14x claim holds only where the small model has non-trivial success.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and gap 6: a weak checker is exploited more as search gets stronger. Allocate budget by estimated difficulty, and stop optimising against the checker on easy items.

source: Wu et al. (2025, ICLR) Inference scaling laws: compute-optimal inference for LLM problem-solving
finding: Compared greedy, majority vote, best-of-n, weighted vote and two tree searches across model sizes at fixed FLOPs. Smaller models with a better search algorithm (REBASE) can beat bigger models with plain sampling at the same compute.
numbers: Llemma-7B with REBASE reaches accuracy competitive with Llemma-34B using about 2x less FLOPs (MATH500, GSM8K). Llemma-7B with REBASE beats Llemma-34B with standard majority voting at all compute budgets.
limits: Math tasks with a trained reward model. Not scientific discovery. Single model family.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 and gap 10: at equal compute, search structure can matter more than model size, but only when a usable reward signal exists.

source: Wang et al. (2024, ICLR) Hypothesis Search: Inductive reasoning with language models (re-read of the ARC table and text)
finding: Re-read Table 1 and the text. Confirmed: human-written hypotheses 45%. The ladder is direct 17, program only 23, summarised hypotheses 30, human-selected 33, human-written 45. Icecuber (no LLM) 43%. The count of 64 candidate programs is held constant in several arms, so this is an equal-sample comparison (not equal tokens): 64 direct programs give 23%, while 64 hypotheses summarised to 8 with 8 programs each give 30%.
numbers: ARC, 100 random tasks, GPT-4. GPT-4 produced a correct hypothesis for 49 tasks (human judged); human-selected hypotheses then solved 33 of 49 (67%). Of 30 tasks solved with summarised hypotheses, 28 had a correct hypothesis before summarising. Execution-feedback rounds, human-written: 38, 44, 45, 45 over rounds 0 to 3. Parsel combinatorial search lifted human-written to 47.5% but hurt LLM-written hypotheses.
limits: Token counts not equalised (the hypothesis step adds tokens). One model. 100 tasks. Human annotators judged hypotheses.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: at the same program count, a short hypothesis layer beats raw program sampling. The limit is hypothesis quality (49 of 100), so selecting the right hypothesis is the lever.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Hypothesis Search, other datasets (SyGuS and List Functions)
finding: The earlier unverified SyGuS 94.3% figure is now confirmed from Table 4, but the hypothesis layer added nothing there: Program Only and Full are both 94.3%. On List Functions the layer helped. An explicit hypothesis step pays only when direct programs are hard.
numbers: SyGuS (89 tasks): CrossBeam 74.8, Program Only 94.3, Full 94.3 (three of the five failures traced to wrong examples). List Functions (100 tasks): Direct 31, Program Only 59, Full 69. SyGuS used 8 programs and 2 feedback rounds, or 4 hypotheses times 2 programs.
limits: GPT-4 only. The CrossBeam comparison uses 50K DSL candidates, not equal compute.
agent_relevance: Do not add a hypothesis stage by default. Use it when direct attempts fail, and spend the saved tokens on more attempts when they succeed.

source: Ma et al. (2024, ICLR) Eureka: Human-level reward design via coding LLMs, ablations
finding: Equal-sample ablation: evolution beats breadth. Eureka with 2 iterations (2 x 16 = 32 reward samples) beat a version that sampled 32 first-attempt rewards with no evolution. Reward reflection (a text summary of how each reward component behaved) matters: removing it cut the average normalised score by 28.6%. Swapping GPT-4 for GPT-3.5 lowers scores but still matches or beats humans on most Isaac tasks.
numbers: Search: 5 iterations, K=16 samples per iteration. Beats human rewards on 83% of tasks, average normalised gain 52%. No-reflection ablation: -28.6% average normalised score over Isaac tasks.
limits: Budget is measured in reward samples, not tokens. Reflection feedback is rich because the RL return is a real checker. Authors' own results.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: with a strong checker, depth (iterate on the best candidate with rich feedback) beats the same number of fresh samples. Keep detailed feedback.

source: Lange, Imajuku, Cetin (2025) ShinkaEvolve: Open-ended and sample-efficient program evolution
finding: An open-source evolutionary coding agent reaches a circle-packing record in 150 samples, where AlphaEvolve-style systems needed thousands. Ablations on circle packing: weighted parent sampling beats best-of-N (always mutate the seed) and hill climbing (which plateaus early); embedding-based novelty rejection with an LLM judge strongly beats none; a bandit over several LLMs beats a single small LLM (GPT-5-nano) and slightly beats a fixed ensemble.
numbers: Circle packing n=26: sum of radii 2.635983 in 150 generations, above the AlphaEvolve score the paper cites. Novelty similarity threshold 0.95. Ablation values are plotted, not tabulated; no single percentage was read.
limits: The ensemble uses frontier models (GPT-5, o4-mini, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 2.5). No run with only a small open model at an equal token budget. Ablations on one task.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 and gap 10: rejecting near-duplicate proposals and balancing exploit/explore saves samples. A small model alone was the weak baseline, so small-model parity is not shown.

source: Novikov et al. (2025) AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery (ablations section)
finding: Ablations on matrix-multiplication tensor decomposition and kissing numbers: removing evolution, prompt context, meta-prompt evolution, full-file evolution, or using a single small base LLM each lowers the result. The authors' own comparison table says FunSearch used small LLMs with no benefit from larger ones, while AlphaEvolve benefits from stronger models.
numbers: Results are in Figure 8 as curves over compute, three seeds each; no single table number. Comparison table: FunSearch used millions of LLM samples, AlphaEvolve thousands.
limits: Authors' own, closed models (Gemini 2.0 Flash and Pro). The 'Small base LLM only' arm is described but no exact numeric gap was extracted.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: direction is clear (stronger or mixed models help at an equal evaluation budget in AlphaEvolve) but the size is not given as a number. Gap stays open for small open models.

source: Romera-Paredes et al. (2024, Nature) Mathematical discoveries from program search with LLMs (FunSearch), PubMed Central full text
finding: Primary now opened. FunSearch uses a pretrained code LLM with no fine-tuning, an island population, and best-shot prompting. The authors chose a fast-inference model over a slower, better one. They report results are not too sensitive to the exact LLM if it was trained on enough code, and point to a StarCoder comparison in Supplementary Appendix A (not opened).
numbers: About 10^6 samples in total. Cap set in dimension n=8: a set of 512 vectors, larger than the previous best known, found as a program. Models: Codey (PaLM 2 based) and open-source StarCoder.
quote: the results obtained in this paper are not too sensitive to the exact choice of LLM
limits: The StarCoder comparison and per-model numbers sit in the Supplementary Information, which was not read. The insensitivity claim is the authors' own and sits against AlphaEvolve's reading of larger-model benefit in a harder setting.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: small and open code models worked in FunSearch at a very large sample count (about a million). Whether a small open model holds at a few thousand samples is untested.

source: Wen et al. (2025) Predicting empirical AI research outcomes with language models
finding: A judge test against external truth: given two ideas, predict which scores higher once actually run. Off-the-shelf frontier models are near chance. A fine-tuned GPT-4.1 with paper retrieval reaches 77% on 1,585 test pairs and beats 25 human experts on NLP, but drops to 63.6% on 33 genuinely new ideas whose results took experts about 103 hours each.
numbers: Zero-shot GPT-4.1 51.9%; o1 and o3 similar or slightly above; fine-tuned system 77% on published pairs; NLP subset system 64.4% vs experts 48.9% (majority aggregate), best-annotator ceiling 60.0%. Unpublished ideas: 63.6% (about 21 of 33). Inter-annotator agreement 75.1%.
quote: off-the-shelf frontier LMs like o3 perform no better than random guessing
limits: Fine-tuned on 6,000 past pairs; off-the-shelf judges alone are not validated. 33 pairs is small (wide interval). AI research ideas only, binary comparison.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: an untrained model judge ranks about at chance against external outcomes. Ranking works only after learning from real outcomes. Never rely on a plain self-judge to pick hypotheses.

source: King et al. (2004, Nature) Functional genomic hypothesis generation and experimentation by a robot scientist (abstract via Europe PMC)
finding: The first robot-scientist test of experiment choice. On reconstructing the aromatic amino acid pathway model in yeast, an intelligent, cost-aware experiment selection strategy was competitive with human selection and clearly cheaper than both cheapest-first and random selection.
numbers: Cost decrease of 3-fold and 100-fold against cheapest-experiment and random-experiment selection. The abstract lists the two baselines as 'cheapest and random' and gives the folds 'respectively', so likely 3-fold vs cheapest and 100-fold vs random; the order was not confirmed in the body.
quote: significantly outperforms, with a cost decrease of 3-fold and 100-fold (respectively), both cheapest and random-experiment selection
limits: Only the abstract was read; the full paper is paywalled. One pathway. The cost unit and the pairing of fold to baseline need the body.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 mostly closed: active choice beat random by about 100x in cost in the original test. Cost-aware choice of the next check beats random choice when checks have unequal costs.

source: Williams et al. (2015) Cheaper faster drug development validated by the repositioning of drugs against neglected tropical diseases (Eve)
finding: Eve picks compounds with active learning on quantitative structure-activity models, mixing exploration and exploitation. The case that it beats brute-force screening comes from an economic model replayed on real screens (14,400 Maybridge compounds), not a head-to-head physical run. The first mass-screen subset is chosen randomly.
numbers: Replay on a P. vivax DHFR screen: cost-optimal to screen between a third and a half of the small library. Intelligent screening is economical under most cost settings (Figure 8). Savings scale with library size under an iid assumption. The Johns Hopkins library (about 1,600 compounds) was judged too small to test.
limits: One example run is shown in the main text; other targets are in the supplement. Library order was a constant random order, so a smarter fixed order was not compared. No hit-recovery percentage versus random was given in the text.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: active selection wins on cost in simulation, with weak physical proof. Claim only 'saves checks when checks are costly', not 'finds more'.

source: Sparkes et al. (2010) Towards robot scientists for autonomous scientific discovery (Adam and Eve review)
finding: Review by the Adam team. Adam identified twelve genes for locally orphan enzymes in yeast through abductive hypotheses, robot-run growth experiments and logic-based records. The review says the systems are not yet cost-effective against human scientists.
numbers: Twelve genes (review wording). Claim K23 said six; the King 2009 abstract (via Europe PMC) says Adam's conclusions were confirmed by manual experiments but gives no count. Formal record: over 10,000 research units, 10 levels deep, 6.6 million biomass measurements.
limits: Review, not the 2009 paper. The 2009 full text was not available, so 12 versus 6 is unresolved: possibly 12 hypotheses with 6 confirmed.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: no random-choice comparison could be read for Adam. Only the 2004 paper gives such a number. Do not claim Adam showed an advantage for active choice.

source: Kulkarni and Simon (1988) The processes of scientific discovery: the strategy of experimentation (abstract via Crossref)
finding: Only the abstract could be reached. KEKADA models Krebs's 1932 urea-cycle heuristics. It reacts to surprises, forms explanations and carries out experiments as the notebooks and interviews show Krebs did. The authors ask how domain-specific and how idiosyncratic the heuristics are, and conclude the control structure and its domain-independent heuristics model scientific experimentation broadly.
numbers: No heuristic list, experiment counts or goal-setting rules were readable. The publisher site and the ScienceDirect copy both blocked access.
quote: KEKADA reacts to surprises, formulates explanations, and carries out experiments
limits: Abstract only. Gap 2 stays open: the surprise rules cannot be specified from this text. Note the DOI suffix is cog1202_1 (a prior attempt with _4 was wrong).
agent_relevance: The abstract confirms surprise leads to explanation goals, and says the heuristics are mostly general. Details for the impasse trigger still need the full paper.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: Updating beliefs from feedback over rounds is weak in off-the-shelf LLMs. In a five-round flight-recommendation task most models improved little after the first round, and chain-of-thought prompting and other prompt changes gave no meaningful gain. Fine-tuning on the Bayesian assistant's predictions improved updating much more than fine-tuning on correct answers, and transferred to new tasks.
numbers: 624 simulated users; five rounds; 100 held-out flight sets evaluated after each round. The Bayesian assistant reaches about 80% final-round accuracy; off-the-shelf LLMs are considerably lower (per-model values are plotted in Figure 2, not read as a table). Bayesian-tuned models agree with the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time.
limits: Stationary preferences, not contradicting data against an accepted theory. A training fix, not a scaffold fix.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: indirect evidence that LLMs stop updating after one round of feedback. A scaffold must force the revision step; prompting alone did not produce it.

source: Tang, Key, Ellis (2024) WorldCoder: a model-based LLM agent that builds world models by writing code
finding: Closest measured case of online revision. The agent writes a Python world model, and when the model fails on stored experience it is re-prompted with the transitions the program gets wrong and asked to debug. This learns Sokoban quickly and transfers to a changed game (teleport gates) by editing the code. A ReAct-style baseline with the same pretrained knowledge fails.
numbers: ReAct solves only 15% (+-8%) of basic Sokoban levels. WorldCoder front-loads about 400k LLM tokens (about $15), then acts with no further LLM cost. Deep RL needs over 1 million steps on 2-box Sokoban.
limits: Deterministic, symbolic, discrete worlds only; GPT-4; authors' own. Revision is triggered by hard counterexamples, not by noisy data.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly answered: revising an accepted model works when failures are exact counterexamples fed back verbatim. A usable pattern for the impasse trigger.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Self-Discover: LLMs self-compose reasoning structures
finding: A fixed library of 39 reasoning modules is the nearest published test of 'a short table of heuristics beats free reasoning'. The model selects, adapts and implements modules once per task, then reuses that structure on every instance. Each of the three steps adds accuracy. It beats chain of thought and beats inference-heavy self-consistency at far lower cost.
numbers: BBH (23 tasks): +7 and +6 points over chain of thought and Plan-and-Solve on PaLM 2-L; +6 and +8 on GPT-4. Over 20% above CoT self-consistency in the abstract, using 10-40x fewer inference calls. Gains largest on world-knowledge tasks (sports, movies, ruin names).
limits: Modules are generic problem-solving prompts, not data-signal triggers like BACON. Tasks are reasoning benchmarks, not law finding. No comparison to a random module choice was found.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 partial and gap 7: a heuristic library chosen per task helps at low cost. It does not show that a signal-to-operator table works for law finding, and operator order was not tested.
